title: The balance
hook: He set the balance, so don't transgress it: weigh justly (55:7–9)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the opening of Ar-Rahman: the Merciful taught, and your line was taught to speak. Did your kind sentence reach the person it was for? Day six hundred four.

At a market stall, a woman scoops lentils onto an old brass scale. The pan dips, she adds a pinch, takes a pinch away, and waits until the needle sits dead center. The customer watches the needle, not her face. Everyone at a scale knows how easy it is to lean a thumb on the pan. Surah Ar-Rahman, a few verses after speech, lifts its eyes to the whole sky. And then, in the very same breath, it comes straight back down to that brass scale on the market stall.
screen: `A BRASS SCALE AT A MARKET STALL.`

segments.voice: Verses seven to nine. Pickthall: "And the sky He hath uplifted; and He hath set the measure, That ye exceed not the measure, But observe the measure strictly, nor fall short thereof." Pickthall says measure; the Arabic word is mizan, and it appears three times in three short verses. Mizan comes from the root w-z-n, to weigh. A mizan is a balance, a pair of scales. Look at what sits side by side. A sky raised high, and a balance set down. Commentators read the first mizan as the order God built into creation: everything in proportion, nothing out of place. Then the next two verses turn it into a command for people. Don't transgress in the balance. Set up the weight with justice, and don't make the balance short. The cosmic order and the shopkeeper's scale are the same word. Cheating at a scale isn't a small thing in this picture; it's a crack in the order that holds up the sky. The Qur'an returns to this often. Surah Al-Mutaffifin opens with woe to those who take full measure for themselves and give short measure to others. The prophet Shu'ayb told his people again and again to give full measure and weight. And the Mizan has one more meaning. On the Day of Judgment, the Qur'an says, God will set up just scales, and no soul will be wronged in the least. So the word stretches from the stars, to the market, to the last day: one balance, kept fair at every size.
screen: `MIZAN: FROM W-Z-N, TO WEIGH.` · `THE SKY RAISED, THE BALANCE SET.` · `DON'T MAKE THE BALANCE SHORT.` · `JUST SCALES ON THE LAST DAY.`

segments.voice: The practice: keep one balance fair. Sit, and let your breath even out, in and out the same length, like two pans settling. Then think of one place in your life where a scale tips your way a little: work you claim, time you take, a share you split, praise you hand out unevenly. Picture setting the needle back to center. Decide on one small correction you'll make today. The bell holds the time.
Mizan. The balance, from the root to weigh: the order of creation, the honest scale, and the just scales of the last day. Today's word.
Your line: keep the balance. Today, make your one correction, even if no one is watching the needle. Day six hundred four.

howItsDone: Islamic law has long treated honest weights and measures as a religious duty; historically a market inspector, the muhtasib, checked traders' scales, and many Muslims recite these verses of Ar-Rahman as a reminder of fair dealing.

original.note: Arabic: the balance, the scales. From the root w-z-n, to weigh.

trapdoor: what you thought: a verse about honest shopkeeping.
what it means: the same word names the order of the sky and the fairness of a scale.
what a scholar hears: mizan, from w-z-n, three times in 55:7–9; commentators link it to justice ('adl), and the plural mawazin names the scales of the Day of Judgment (21:47).
